opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot. The classic next-token prediction objective has been remarkably powerful. It gives you broad world knowledge, fluency, and a surprising amount of reasoning ability just from compressing the internet. But when you want a model to act as an agent, to plan over many steps, call tools, observe what happens, and recover from mistakes, you start to see the limits of a purely passive objective.

The way I frame it is that pre-training on static text teaches the model what the world *looks like*, but not necessarily what happens when *you act on it*. Most web text is the end product of some process. You see the finished code, not the twenty failed attempts and the debugging in between. You see the final answer, not the search that led there. So one direction is to bring more process data into pre-training: execution traces, interaction logs, code alongside its outputs and error messages, multi-turn trajectories where the state actually changes in response to actions.

A second piece is the horizon of the objective. Next-token prediction is very local. For agentic behavior you care about whether a sequence of decisions leads somewhere good many steps later. There's interesting work on multi-token prediction, on objectives that encourage the model to represent longer-range plans, and on mixing in signals that look more like goal-conditioned prediction. I don't think we've found the definitive answer there yet, but I'm fairly convinced the objective should reward some notion of lookahead, not just the immediate next token.

Then there's the boundary between pre-training and post-training, which I think is getting blurrier. Historically we'd pre-train on a huge corpus and then do instruction tuning and RL at the end to teach behavior. For agents, it may make sense to introduce interactive or environment-grounded data much earlier, so those capabilities are part of the model's foundation rather than a thin layer on top. If the base model already has good priors about acting, observing, and revising, RL in post-training becomes far more sample-efficient, because you're refining a behavior rather than inventing it.

And finally, scale and data quality still matter enormously. A lot of what we learned from training very large models is that capabilities like multi-step reasoning show up more reliably at scale and with the right data mixture, especially lots of high-quality code and math. Code in particular is a wonderful substrate for agents: it's structured, it's executable, and it gives you a ground-truth signal about whether an action worked. So if I had to bet, the pre-training recipe for agentic models will look like next-token prediction as the backbone, enriched with much more interaction and execution data, some form of longer-horizon objective, and a tighter coupling with the RL stage that follows.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction has been remarkably powerful for fluency and describes it as the backbone of the recipe, conveying its fit for generating text.

r002.rationale: It says agents must plan over many steps, call tools, observe outcomes, and recover from mistakes—capabilities beyond passive text prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I think the pre-training objective itself is less of the story than people assume, and the data mixture and the post-training are more of it.

Next-token prediction is a remarkably general objective. When you train on a broad enough corpus, you're implicitly learning a lot of things an agent needs: how procedures are described, how code calls into tools, how people reason step by step through a problem, how an error message maps back to a cause. So I don't think the right framing is "we need a new objective for agents." The question is what the model is seeing during pre-training, and whether the kinds of behaviors you want at inference time are actually represented in that distribution.

That said, there are real gaps. Pre-training data is mostly the output of a process, not the process. You see the finished Stack Overflow answer, not the twelve things someone tried before they got there. You see the final essay, not the drafts. For an agent, the trajectory matters: taking an action, observing something, updating, and acting again. That loop is underrepresented on the web, so you tend to get models that are great at producing a plausible-looking plan and much weaker at recovering when step three doesn't go the way the plan said it would.

So the way I think about it is in layers. First, during pre-training, be deliberate about including data that looks like interaction: code with execution traces, tool calls with returned results, long multi-step documents where state evolves. Second, long context becomes a first-class concern, because an agent's working memory is its context window. If the model can't attend reliably to something from two thousand steps ago, no amount of clever prompting fixes that. Third, the objective shifts closer to the agentic setting in post-training, where you can actually ground it in outcomes: did the task get done, did the tests pass, did the environment reach the right state. That's where reinforcement learning on real or simulated environments earns its keep.

The caution I'd add is that it's tempting to over-engineer the pre-training objective toward agents and lose the generality that made these models useful in the first place. The thing that makes a good agent is largely the same thing that makes a good language model: broad world knowledge, strong reasoning, and calibrated uncertainty about what it doesn't know. I'd rather preserve that and add the agentic skills on top than bake narrow behaviors in early and discover later that they don't transfer.

r001.rationale: It calls next-token prediction a general objective, but does not explain that it is naturally suited to generating text.

r002.rationale: It describes agent needs beyond producing text, including taking actions, observing results, adapting, using tools, and completing tasks in an environment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do we want the model to learn during pre-training that will be useful when it has to take actions? Predicting the next token gives you a very general learning signal. You can learn from language, code, and sequences that describe actions and their outcomes. But being good at predicting those sequences doesn’t automatically mean you’re good at choosing actions to accomplish a goal.

For an agent, you also care about how it uses feedback. Can it recognize that an action didn’t work, revise its approach, and continue? Can it decide when it needs more information or when it should call a tool? So I would think about both the objective and the data: does the training experience expose the model to those interactions and their consequences?

And then there’s the question of what belongs in pre-training versus post-training. Pre-training can provide a broad foundation, while training with interaction and feedback can help connect that foundation to successful behavior. Ultimately, you need to evaluate whether the model completes the task, not just whether it produces a plausible description of what to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes next-token prediction as a general learning signal and says it can learn from language, but does not clearly explain that it is naturally suited to generating text.

r002.rationale: The response says predicting sequences does not automatically make a model good at choosing actions to accomplish a goal, and identifies feedback, revising actions, and tool use as agent needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what do we want the model to learn before we ask it to act? Predicting the next token gives us a very general learning objective. The model can learn language, acquire knowledge, and pick up patterns of reasoning. But an agent also needs to choose actions, observe what happens, and adjust its behavior over multiple steps.

So I would think about both the objective and the data. If the training data includes sequences of observations, actions, and outcomes, then prediction can teach the model something about interaction. But predicting an action in a recorded trajectory doesn’t necessarily mean the model can choose the right action when its own decisions change what happens next.

That’s where I think you need to connect pre-training with learning from interaction and feedback. Pre-training gives you a broad foundation; subsequent training can help align action selection with successful outcomes. And the evaluation has to reflect that distinction: does the model just produce a plausible next step, or can it actually complete the task and recover when something goes wrong?

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction can teach language and reasoning, but does not clearly explain that it is naturally suited to generating text.

r002.rationale: It says agents must choose actions, observe outcomes, and adjust over multiple steps, going beyond simply producing text.
